title: Things to do in Ferrara: 5 places from castle to city walls
description: Plan five Ferrara visits: the Este Castle, cathedral, Palazzo dei Diamanti, Schifanoia and city walls, with museum choices, transport and access advice.
relatedQueries: Ferrara castle palaces and city walls
intro: For a first visit to Ferrara, connect five places that explain different stages of the city: the Este Castle, the cathedral beside Piazza Trento e Trieste, Palazzo dei Diamanti, Palazzo Schifanoia and the city walls. Their interest lies in the connections between a ruling family’s fortress, religious spaces, Renaissance palaces and a green belt. You can experience a substantial part of the route from the streets, choosing the interiors that match your interests.

Ferrara was inscribed on the World Heritage List as a Renaissance city in 1995; the designation was extended in 1999 to the Po Delta territory and the Delizie Estensi. This guide concentrates on the city, without treating that wider territory as an excursion to fit into the same day. Official information was consulted on 15 November 2026. Calendars, restoration works and the areas open to visitors need a final check for your actual travel date.

quickFacts.label: Orientation point
quickFacts.value: The Este Castle is a useful reference between the historic centre and Corso Ercole I d’Este.

quickFacts.label: Northern route
quickFacts.value: Corso Ercole I d’Este connects the castle, the Palazzo dei Diamanti area and Porta degli Angeli.

quickFacts.label: Schifanoia Museum
quickFacts.value: The address is via Scandiana 23; allow a separate visiting block for its collection.

quickFacts.label: City walls
quickFacts.value: The historic green belt is about nine kilometres long: choose a section rather than assuming you must complete the circuit.

quickFacts.label: Reservations and tickets
quickFacts.value: A free Schifanoia reservation does not mean free admission; the museum states that tickets are bought at its ticket office.

sections.heading: 1. Este Castle: from a defensive moat to a court residence
paragraphs: The castle is a useful starting point because it makes the relationship between political power and the city visible. Nicolò II d’Este ordered the fortress in 1385 after an uprising, with a design by Bartolino da Novara. Its moat, bridges and four corner towers help you recognize that defensive purpose. Over time, the family transformed the complex into a court residence, adding balconies, ceremonial spaces and decoration. First look at the building from different sides of its perimeter: the interiors then become part of a developing residence rather than a disconnected sequence of rooms.

If you go inside, distinguish the museum route from the arrangements for the Torre dei Leoni and the prisons. The general tourism description lists historic spaces, but the castle’s own opening page publishes restrictions for the prisons; a description does not establish that every area is available. The accessibility guide also excludes the prisons and tower from the accessible museum route. It identifies wheelchair access through San Paolo Tower, on the south-west side, with a lift to the first floor. Check the route currently operating and the last admission before buying, particularly if the tower is your main reason for visiting.

sections.heading: 2. Cathedral and Piazza Trento e Trieste: understanding the medieval centre
paragraphs: The Cathedral of San Giorgio Martire provides a useful contrast with the fortress. Construction dates to 1135, and its façade combines Romanesque and Gothic phases: avoid reading the whole building as the result of a single campaign. From the squares, look at the façade, its relationship with the town hall and the side facing Piazza Trento e Trieste. Changing your viewpoint helps reveal the cathedral’s place in the everyday urban setting alongside its religious purpose.

The municipal information consulted describes restoration work inside the building. This stop therefore also works as an exterior visit: a worship schedule or archive photograph does not guarantee access to every area, an unobstructed façade or an absence of works. Check notices and respect services if you enter. Also distinguish the cathedral from the separate Cathedral Museum across the square in the former church of San Romano; its visiting arrangements are independent. For a pause between museum visits, the public urban space already provides historical context without requiring another admission ticket.

sections.heading: 3. Palazzo dei Diamanti: a façade that explains Renaissance expansion
paragraphs: Follow Corso Ercole I d’Este towards Palazzo dei Diamanti. The avenue links the castle with Porta degli Angeli in the city walls and crosses the Quadrivio degli Angeli. This junction helps explain the Addizione Erculea, the urban extension associated with Ercole I and Biagio Rossetti. The palace takes its name from more than 8,500 pointed marble blocks on its exterior. Watch how light changes their relief, and look at the corner in relation to the crossroads, rather than limiting your attention to a straight-on photograph.

The building has distinct functions that matter when choosing admission. Temporary exhibitions occupy the ground floor, while the upper floor houses the Pinacoteca Nazionale. Seeing the façade from the street, visiting an exhibition and exploring the national gallery are different experiences. Check the current programme and what your chosen ticket includes instead of assuming combined access. For exhibitions, the operator explains that online reservations correspond to a selected date and admission slot. It also publishes accessibility information, accessible toilet facilities and wheelchair loans subject to availability. Choosing the interior before your trip avoids buying an exhibition ticket simply because you recognize the palace’s name.

sections.heading: 4. Palazzo Schifanoia: looking at the frescoes with context
paragraphs: Palazzo Schifanoia is the selection here for exploring the culture of the Este court in greater depth. Its origins date to around 1385 under Alberto V d’Este, with an enlargement promoted by Borso from 1466. The museum renewed in 2021 presents about 250 works in 21 rooms, including paintings, sculpture, ceramics, medals and illuminated manuscripts. The Salone dei Mesi connects the court’s political life with the solar year, astrology and mythology. Seven of the original twelve monthly sections survive: knowing this helps interpret the paintings without expecting an intact, complete pictorial calendar.

Arrive at via Scandiana 23 with time for the museum route rather than only an exterior photograph. The museum recommends free reservations for individuals and groups, but its accessibility page clarifies that admission tickets are bought at the ticket office. The ordinary hours consulted are Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00–19:00, with last admission at 18:00 and Monday closure; a separate calendar lists exceptional openings, so check your date. There are lifts, tactile resources and subtitled videos. Moving between the mezzanine and main floor can require changing wings through the ground floor: examine the map if these internal connections affect your visit.

sections.heading: 5. Ferrara’s city walls: choosing a section of the green belt
paragraphs: The walls help you appreciate the scale of the city you have been exploring. The circuit forms a green belt of about nine kilometres, with walking and cycle paths, bastions, towers and gates from different periods. Medieval origins and changes in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries show how the defences adapted to urban expansion. Today, the interest lies in those structures and in the wooded areas and changing perspectives along the paths. A section outdoors can provide a welcome contrast to a day focused on museum interiors.

You do not need to complete the circuit for the stop to be worthwhile. From Diamanti, Corso Ercole I d’Este points towards Porta degli Angeli, the former northern entrance to the Addizione Erculea fortifications. Use the official map to choose an entrance and exit, then plan the return to your accommodation or the station separately. The municipal itineraries describe different sectors; they do not guarantee uniform access, an absence of works or adapted surfaces at every connection. Share paths carefully with cyclists, and change the section if the ground conditions, rain or your group’s mobility needs make a different route more practical.

sections.heading: Arriving in Ferrara and connecting the sightseeing blocks
paragraphs: First organize your arrival at Ferrara station, then the connection to your intended starting point. The operators’ guides link Trenitalia, Italo and Tper services, but a list of companies does not establish a direct connection or a journey time from every origin. Look up the specific departure, its changes and the return covered by your ticket. If your journey continues through Italy, the Bologna, Padua and Venice guides can help with those separate stages, each with its own checked or reserved transport.

Divide sightseeing into areas. The castle and cathedral form the central group; Corso Ercole, Diamanti and the northern wall access form another axis. Schifanoia deserves its own block in via Scandiana. The Diamanti operator suggests bus 3 from the station and bus 4 for the return, while Schifanoia lists other routes and final walking sections. Check current stops and services with Tper before setting off. If you hire a bicycle, verify rental conditions, parking and traffic rules: the presence of cycle paths does not turn every pavement or museum approach into a place to ride.

sections.heading: Admission, access and a realistic selection of museums
paragraphs: Choose the main interior for the day according to your interests: the castle for its transformation from fortress to court residence, Schifanoia for its frescoes and collections, or a specific exhibition at Diamanti. Add a second museum only when its opening arrangements and your available time allow you to give it attention. One institution’s weekly closure does not establish the others: the castle publishes an ordinary Tuesday closure and Schifanoia a Monday closure, with exceptions to check. Look at the last admission and the areas available as well as the closing time. Meals and breaks need their own margin.

Access needs vary between the places too. The castle distinguishes the museum, tower and prisons; Schifanoia describes lifts in different wings, toilet facilities and interpretation resources; Diamanti publishes services for visitors with reduced mobility. Confirm the route you would actually use and ask staff for information when a detail determines whether the visit is practical. In wet weather, keep the wall section flexible and prioritize the interiors you have chosen. Fixed prices are not listed here because they depend on the museum, exhibition, ticket type and current concessions: identifying the appropriate ticket is more useful than a general figure that may not apply.

itinerary: Central block: begin around the Este Castle and decide whether to take its interior route. Continue towards the cathedral and Piazza Trento e Trieste, adapting any entry to services, notices and the areas open to visitors. This first group helps you understand the centre before committing the rest of your day.

Renaissance and green block: follow Corso Ercole I d’Este to Palazzo dei Diamanti. If you have chosen an exhibition or the national gallery, allow a separate visiting window for it. Then add a wall section from the Porta degli Angeli area, returning through a point identified on the map.

Schifanoia block: give via Scandiana and the museum another window, especially if the frescoes are your priority. During a short single-day visit, choose between this interior and another substantial museum programme; if you have more time, spread the blocks across your stay without a compulsory number of days. Five recommended places do not require five admission purchases.

faq.question: What should I see on a first visit to Ferrara?
faq.answer: This selection brings together the Este Castle, the cathedral and Piazza Trento e Trieste, Palazzo dei Diamanti, Palazzo Schifanoia and the city walls. Combine squares and exteriors with the museum that interests you most. This introduces the medieval and Renaissance city without turning the visit into a succession of rushed admissions.

faq.question: Can I visit all five places in one day?
faq.answer: You can organize exteriors and a wall section around one or two interiors, depending on your actual available time and opening arrangements. That does not mean exploring every museum in depth. Schifanoia needs its own visiting block, while an exhibition at Diamanti can substantially change how you divide the day.

faq.question: Are Palazzo dei Diamanti and the Pinacoteca the same visit?
faq.answer: They share a building, but temporary exhibitions occupy the ground floor while the upper floor houses the Pinacoteca Nazionale. Check the programme, ticket and conditions before buying. Recognizing the façade is not a reason to assume that one admission automatically covers both institutions.

faq.question: Does a free Schifanoia reservation include admission?
faq.answer: The recommended reservation is free, but the museum states that admission tickets are purchased at its ticket office. Do not confuse reserving a place with eligibility for free entry: exemptions depend on visitor circumstances and the published conditions. Also check last admission and exceptions to the ordinary weekly closure.

faq.question: Do I need to walk all nine kilometres of the walls?
faq.answer: No. Choose a section that connects well with your visit and identify its entrance, exit and return journey. From the Diamanti axis, you can head towards Porta degli Angeli. Completing the whole circuit requires more time and a separate decision; path conditions and the group’s needs determine the appropriate section.

conclusion: Ferrara becomes easier to understand when you connect the Este fortress with its palaces, religious centre and green defensive perimeter. Choose interiors for what they contain, check each admission’s conditions and leave time to notice the streets between them. The related Bologna, Padua and Venice guides can help with other Italian stages, each keeping its own sightseeing route and transport arrangements.
